title: The children
hookLine: he let his grandsons Hasan and Husayn climb on him during prayer

cards: The mosque in Medina is full. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is leading the prayer, and the whole congregation goes down into prostration behind him, foreheads to the ground. And they stay down.
It's taking far too long. Has something happened? Has revelation come?
Is he all right? One man lifts his head to look. There, on the Prophet's back, sitting like he's riding a camel, is a small boy, his grandson, very pleased with himself.
The Prophet isn't getting up until the boy is ready to climb off.

teach.h: MY SON WAS RIDING ON ME.
teach.b: The story is in the Sunan of an-Nasa'i. After the prayer, people told him: you made the prostration so long we thought something had happened. He said: none of that happened.
My son was riding on me, and I didn't want to rush him until he'd had enough. The boy was Hasan or Husayn, the sons of his daughter Fatimah; he called his grandsons his sons. It wasn't a one-off.
Sahih al-Bukhari says he sometimes prayed carrying his granddaughter Umamah, putting her down when he bowed and picking her up when he stood.

teach.h: A BABY CRIES, THE PRAYER IS SHORT.
teach.b: He said he'd sometimes start a prayer meaning to make it long, hear a baby crying in the back, and shorten it, because he knew how the mother felt.
Once a man named al-Aqra' saw him kissing Hasan and said, I have ten children and I've never kissed a single one of them. The Prophet said: whoever doesn't show mercy won't be shown mercy.

He noticed children's small worlds, too. A little boy named Abu 'Umayr had a pet bird that died, and every time the Prophet saw him, he'd ask, in a rhyme, O Abu 'Umayr, what happened to the little bird?
And Anas, who worked in his house from the age of about ten, said: I served him for ten years, and he never once said to me, ugh, and never asked why I did something or why I didn't.
Muslims often read these as small stories. They aren't.
A prophet in prayer, the most serious moment of his day, waited for a child.

how: Children are commonly brought to mosques, and many Muslims cite these hadith to argue for welcoming them, tolerating their noise, and treating them with gentleness and affection.

o: the Prophet's teachings on raising children to pray
the orphans the Prophet took into his own home
how the Prophet treated children, with patience and play

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: rode on his back in prostration
carried in his arms in prayer
the boy whose little bird died

s: the Prophet lengthened the prostration for a child
my son was riding on me, and I didn't want to rush him.
he made prayers longer when babies cried
he shortened them, knowing how the mother felt.
Anas said the Prophet never once scolded him with ugh
ten years of service, and never ugh, never why did you or why didn't you.

games.q: you're leading the prayer, in prostration, and your small grandson climbs onto your back. the whole mosque is waiting. what do you do?
o: stand up gently so he slides off.
stay down until he's had enough.
ask someone to take him away.
games.why: he stayed down: my son was riding on me, and I didn't want to rush him until he'd had enough.

practice: Think of a child in your life: your own, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, or the child you once were.

Picture a moment when they slow you down, the endless why, the shoe that won't go on, the story that takes forever, and picture yourself staying down, like the Prophet in prostration, until they're done.

wordCard.voice: The children. How the Prophet was with them: a grandson on his back in prayer, a granddaughter in his arms, a question about a little bird. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Hasan and Husayn, the sons of Fatimah and 'Ali, the Prophet's grandsons.

carryVoice: Your line: the child on his back, and no rush to get up. See you tomorrow.
